what: Planar 3-RPR parallel positioning table. Three motor-driven small linear actuators, legs A, B and C, each join a fixed base hinge to a hinge on one passive triangular platform: revolute–prismatic–revolute. Together the three leg lengths set the platform’s two translations in the horizontal plane (x = LDraw X, y = LDraw Z) and its heading (yaw); a long red pointer, whose tip sits 16 mm to the side of and 80 mm ahead of the platform reference point, makes the yaw visible: during a turn the tip sweeps an arc, so tip motion alone does not show translation. At home every leg is 56 mm (140 LDU) between hinge axes: legs A and C lie along x facing each other, leg B lies along y. Each motor turns its actuator spindle, about 1.21 mm of length per turn. The program converts each target pose into three leg lengths and motor angles and visits 15 poses: ±4.8 mm in x, ±4.8 mm in y, ±10° yaw, four combined poses (±3.2 mm, ±3.2 mm, ±7°) and home between the groups.
try: Reset to the saved pose and press Run. The program refuses to start if any of the three motors is more than 1° away from its saved angle.
During the +x move, watch leg B. Legs A and C change by 4.8 mm in opposite directions; how much does B change?

During the +10° yaw, compare the three legs: all of them lengthen (A and B by about 3.1 mm, C by about 2.8 mm), yet the platform only turns about its reference point. Why does a pure rotation need all three legs to grow?

In the combined poses all three motors move at once with matched travel times. Compare the platform only at the pauses: the path between two poses is not a straight line, because the program interpolates motor angles, not positions.
why: Let a_i be the fixed base hinges, b_i the platform hinges in platform coordinates, t = (x, y) the position of the platform reference point and R(ψ) the rotation by the yaw ψ. The moving hinge is then q_i = t + R(ψ) b_i, and leg i must have the length ρ_i = |q_i − a_i|. This inverse kinematics is direct: choose a pose and compute three distances. The reverse direction is harder: three given lengths can allow more than one assembly of the platform, so the machine must stay on its starting branch and away from singular poses, where the leg directions stop constraining one of the three coordinates and small length changes can cause large platform motion. Because every leg sees every coordinate, no single motor is an x, y or yaw axis. Experimental model: measured only in the simulator (one headless run, from three platform hinge points rather than the encoders), every settled pose was within 0.005 mm and 0.012° of its target and the measured leg lengths matched |q_i − a_i| within 0.002 mm; nothing has been tested on real LEGO parts.
matters: Parallel stages like this position wafers, microscope samples and optics in XY-yaw and, as hexapods, in six axes: the closed chains share the load and are stiff, but the controller must solve the coupled geometry for every move. Triad Table makes that coupling visible with three legs. Its limits are honest ones: there are no physical stops for yaw, the supplier qualified only the programmed route, and the real actuators’ clutches, play and cable routing have not been tested.
question: During the +4.8 mm move in x, leg A grows by 4.8 mm and leg C shrinks by 4.8 mm. How much must leg B change, and could motor B simply stay still?
answer: Leg B is perpendicular to the motion, so its length changes only to second order: √(56² + 4.8²) − 56 ≈ 0.205 mm, about 61° of its motor. It still has to move: if B stayed fixed, the platform could not reach the pure translation and would be pulled sideways or turned. That is why no single motor acts as an independent x axis.
further: Predict the leg lengths for a pure +10° yaw from the anchors in the formula; compare with A = B ≈ 59.08 mm and C ≈ 58.78 mm.

Compare Twinpoint, which positions a single point with two motors in a five-bar loop; Atlas Six, which adds height, pitch and roll with six legs; and Axis Plotter, a serial Cartesian stage where each motor really is one axis.

Find the singular configurations on paper: when the three leg lines meet in one point, the platform can turn about that point without any leg changing length to first order; when all three are parallel, it can shift sideways in the same way.
formula: q_i = t + R(ψ) b_i; ρ_i = |q_i − a_i|. Base anchors a_A = (−180, −40), a_B = (40, −180), a_C = (140, 40) LDU; platform anchors b_A = (−40, −40), b_B = (40, −40), b_C = (0, 40) LDU; home ρ = 140 LDU = 56 mm (1 LDU = 0.4 mm). Motor angle_i = 360° × (ρ_i − 140 LDU) / 3.0147 LDU per spindle turn; e.g. +12 LDU (4.8 mm) → 1433°. Positive yaw turns +x towards +y.
